annotations.text:
davidparsons.me — three directions

Same real content in all three: your actual bio (employer dropped, 15 years in), the five notes, all 24 talks, the contact form.

These are static mockups for picking a look, not a working site. Once you pick, I build that one in Next.js.

Rows read left to right: Home, Notes, Speaking, Contact.

A — Quiet Index

The site you have now, executed properly. Newsreader serif for prose, IBM Plex Mono for every date and label, one ink on warm paper, no accent colour at all.

Signature: Speaking as a true index — years in the left gutter, venues left, dates right, a hairline between years rather than between rows.

Tradeoff: it's the quietest of the three. If you want the site to look obviously different from 2017, this is the smallest visible change.

B — Standing Rail

Asymmetric: a fixed identity rail on the left carries your name, bio, nav and links on every page; content flows on the right. Space Grotesk set tight, IBM Plex Sans body, one deep teal used only for links and focus.

Signature: the rail marks where you are, and link underlines draw in on hover.

Tradeoff: the rail costs 340px and has to collapse on a phone, so mobile becomes a second layout rather than the same one narrower.

C — Workbench

Ink-dark, mono-forward, two muted accents (cool for links and dates, warm for section labels). Reads like a well-made developer tool.

Signature: a real ⌘K palette that jumps to any page, post or talk — second artboard in this row shows it open.

Tradeoff: dark-only says 'developer tool' more than 'person who writes'; your long conference-notes posts are harder to read on dark. The palette is also real code to build and keep working.
